lines: Here's a real pipeline that only ever writes down how far it's gotten once a batch is genuinely, durably finished, never a moment before that.
Now make it crash, right in the middle of a stream, exactly as its next batch starts going out the door. Does picking back up afterward redo anything it already finished, or lose anything it hadn't?
answer: It picks back up exactly where it genuinely left off, nothing redone, nothing missing.

lines: Run it for real: the record this pipeline wrote down lines up exactly with the last batch it genuinely finished. Picking back up afterward redoes nothing and loses nothing.

Now take the identical real crash, at the identical real moment, against a second pipeline that writes down how far it's gotten the instant a batch is handed off, before it's actually finished at all.
Does that second pipeline's own record still line up with what genuinely happened, or does it get ahead of itself?
answer: It writes down a batch as done one whole step before that batch was ever actually finished.

lines: Run it for real: that second pipeline's own record claims one more batch finished than genuinely was, because the crash landed exactly while that one was still going out the door.
steps.takeaway: Writing something down before it's genuinely finished records a promise the pipeline never actually kept.

lines: When that second pipeline picks back up, it starts right after whatever it wrote down, skipping straight past the one batch that record claims is already handled.
Does that skipped batch's own real data come back later, or is it simply gone?
answer: Picking back up never looks at that batch again, so whatever it held is gone for good.

lines: Run it for real: a whole real batch's worth of records, genuinely never finished, vanishes the moment picking back up resumes, because the record said it was already handled.
steps.takeaway: Writing down too much doesn't redo extra work; it quietly erases whatever was never genuinely finished.

lines: One real, well-known piece of documentation, about making sure a write genuinely reaches disk, describes exactly this distinction in its own words.
A write only counts as genuinely finished once it has actually reached where it's going. Writing something down before that moment is writing down a finish that hasn't happened yet.
steps.takeaway: What a pipeline writes down is only as honest as the work it's supposed to follow, never the work it's merely expecting.

lines: So here's what both of these real runs were really showing: writing something down only once it's genuinely finished lets picking back up continue exactly where things actually stood, nothing redone, nothing missing.
Writing it down a moment too early can look completely identical, right up until something crashes in exactly the wrong place, at which point it quietly erases whatever never actually finished.
Either way, it's the identical real lesson: a record is only ever as true as the real work standing behind it, never the work it merely expects is coming.
